description: The first cluster (red-colored) (n: 20) stresses how travel influencers and bloggers influence the image of a destination and tourists’ post-consumption behavior. No theory dominated the cluster, as most articles lacked a theoretical foundation. Various theories, such as attitude theory, involvement theory, motivation-hygiene theory, and the Realist Evaluation Approach, were applied at least once in this cluster. Regarding context, several articles have analyzed how travel bloggers affect the reputation of individual destinations, including Catalonia (Marine-Roig, 2014), China (Li & Wang, 2011) and Istanbul (Alrawadieh et al., 2018). For instance, Alrawadieh et al. (2018) and Li and Wang (2011) explored how Western travelers viewed Istanbul and China, respectively, while Iordanova and Stainton (2019) established that emotion and trust can lead to shaping travelers’ perception of Cambodia. However, there were no notable unique characteristics in this cluster because the majority of the research relied on different qualitative methods to analyze data from travel blogs and online travel reviews. Studies in this cluster utilized various methodologies to investigate the impact of travel blogs and bloggers on prospective travelers, including content analysis (Alrawadieh et al., 2018; Li & Wang, 2011), realist evaluation (Banyai & Havitz, 2013), and webometric analysis (Marine-Roig, 2014). For example, Tse and Zhang (2013) content analyzed Chinese tourists’ experiences in Hong Kong using blogs and microblogs, while MarineRoig (2014) conducted a webometric analysis of travel blogs and reviews hosted in Catalonia. Finally, these studies employed several methods to examine travel blogs as a source of information for tourists and their impact on destination image and tourist behavior (Li & Wang, 2011).

The second cluster (green-colored) (n: 19) focuses on the impact of influencers on travel decisions and experiences. This cluster is characterized by the application of diverse theoretical perspectives to interpret how SMIs influence travel behavior and decision-making. However, no single theory dominates the cluster. The Stimulus-OrganismResponse (SOR) framework holds particular prominence, with two studies employing it to delve into tourist viewpoints and behavior. For instance, Seçilmiş et al. (2022) utilized the SOR model to examine how environmental stimuli (expertise and attractiveness of travel content) influence emotional responses (cognitive responses and trust), ultimately impacting visit intention. Conversely, Le and Hancer (2021) expanded upon the social learning theory by investigating the desire among YouTube viewers to mimic the travel experiences of vloggers. X. Xu and Pratt (2018) further explored the endorsement of travel destinations through SMIs via the lens of self-congruence theory. This cluster includes research emphasizing specific influencer categories, including Instafamous (FemeniaSerra et al., 2022; Yılmazdoğan et al., 2021), food vloggers (Leung et al., 2022), and travel vloggers (He et al., 2022; Le & Hancer, 2021). This cluster also includes studies that explored the role of influencers in promoting destinations (Yang et al., 2022) and restaurants (Leung et al., 2022). Studies that focused on the COVID-19 period, explicitly analyzing how travel influencers influence visit intention and consumer behavior (Femenia-Serra et al., 2022), are also included in this cluster. In addition, various types of samples were used in this cluster. Aşan (2022) analyzed the impact of travel influencers on bicycle travellers, while, Yılmazdoğan et al. (2021) focused on the influence of source credibility on travel intention toward becoming Instafamous. Previous studies in this cluster have consistently emphasized the significant role influencers play in shaping travel decisions. Many people trust the opinions of travel influencers and rely on them when making decisions about their tourist destinations and activities. Recent statistics reveal that 70% of travelers have confidence in the opinions of travel influencers. Travel influencers, on average, have a 3.6% engagement rate on Instagram, significantly higher than the 1.9% average engagement rate for non-influencer accounts. Additionally, 84% of travel influencers trust the recommendations of fellow travel influencers when planning their trips (Socialstar, 2023). Furthermore, several studies explored the factors that can mediate the impact of influencers on travel behavior, such as the role of trust in tourist decisions (Pop et al., 2022). In addition, this cluster extensively explored the moderating role of gender in understanding how SMI influences consumer behavior within the H&T sector. The studies examined this effect across various contexts, including travel (Le & Hancer, 2021), events (Sun et al., 2021), and restaurant sectors (Leung et al., 2022). Regarding methodology, most research employed quantitative methods, primarily cross-sectional surveys, to analyze the relationships among variables. Additionally, some studies used structural equation modeling (SEM) for a more robust examination of these relationships. However, despite their respective differences, the articles included in this cluster share a mutual interest in comprehending the impact of influencers on shaping travel behavior and decision-making.

The third cluster (blue-colored) (n: 18) combines several studies that highlight the effectiveness of SMPs in understanding tourist-brand relationships. In terms of theoretical grounding, no specific theory or framework dominated the cluster. Most articles lacked a strong theoretical foundation and relied primarily on qualitative data analysis. Conversely, the majority of articles identified the role of leveraging SMPs like Instagram, Sina Weibo, Twitter, and Facebook in promoting destinations, hotels, and the accommodation industry (X. Jin & Cheng, 2020). For example, Barbe et al. (2020) investigated why users follow travel accounts on Instagram. Several studies in this cluster focused on how SMPs influence consumer behavior in the H&T industry (G. McCartney & R. C. Pek, 2018; Mich & Baggio, 2015). These studies revealed the influence of Sina Weibo travel blogs on sentiment toward hotel accommodations in Macau (G. McCartney & R. C. Pek, 2018) and the effects of Facebook pages of small-scale hotels on customer attitudes (Mich & Baggio, 2015). Research also investigated the role of SMPs in promoting mega-events (X. Jin & Cheng, 2020) and utilizing Twitter data for marketing in cruise tourism (Park et al., 2016). Studies in this cluster concluded that SMP is an effective tool for supporting destination marketing, sharing knowledge and ideas about travel products, and promoting user-generated content. Lastly, content analysis and thematic analysis were the most popular methods in this cluster, both methods offering valuable insights into user behavior, opinions, and trends on SMPs and travel websites (Fath et al., 2017; G. McCartney & R. C. Pek, 2018). In this cluster, these methods were applied to various social media sites, including Twitter, Facebook, and Sina Weibo.

The fourth cluster (yellow-colored) (n: 5) focuses on IM practices, features in influencer posts that grab viewers’ attention, and how customers react to these messages. For example, Deng et al. (2022) studied how people reacted to wine videos by influencers on TikTok. Their findings indicated that the product stood out the most for men and millennials. However, the influencer had the most significant impact on females. P.-Y. Lee et al. (2021) reported similar results when they examined the mostviewed and most-commented points in photos shared by Instafamous that the influencers attract more attention than what is being promoted by influencers. Studies in this cluster also investigated how Instagram and blog posts affect followers’ perception of a destination (Gholamhosseinzadeh et al., 2023) and how visitors perceive a destination’s unique promise (Martin et al., 2007). This cluster lacks prominent theories, contextual frameworks, or characteristics. Additionally, the sample size is relatively small, making generalizations based on the TCCM framework less reliable. Regarding methodology, the studies employ diverse analytical approaches, including content analysis, topic modeling, and narrative analysis, which collectively offer a comprehensive lens to analyze and interpret the varied content shared on SMP and travel blogs. In conclusion, studies in this cluster investigated how consumers or tourists respond to IM efforts by destinations or businesses.
